In [[measure theory]], a field of mathematics, the '''Hausdorff density''' measures how concentrated a [[Radon measure]] is at some point.

== Definition ==

Let <math>\mu</math> be a Radon measure and <math>a\in\mathbb{R}^{n}</math> some point in [[Euclidean space]]. The ''s''-dimensional upper and lower Hausdorff densities are defined to be, respectively, 
:<math> \Theta^{*s}(\mu,a)=\limsup_{r\rightarrow 0}\frac{\mu(B_{r}(a))}{r^{s}}</math>
and
:<math> \Theta_{*}^{s}(\mu,a)=\liminf_{r\rightarrow 0}\frac{\mu(B_{r}(a))}{r^{s}}</math>
where <math> B_{r}(a)</math> is the [[ball (mathematics)|ball]] of radius ''r'' > 0 centered at ''a''. Clearly, <math>\Theta_{*}^{s}(\mu,a)\leq \Theta^{*s}(\mu,a)</math> for all <math>a\in\mathbb{R}^{n}</math>. In the event that the two are equal, we call their common value the '''s-density''' of <math>\mu</math> at ''a'' and denote it <math>\Theta^{s}(\mu,a)</math>.

== Marstrand's theorem ==

The following theorem states that the times when the ''s''-density exists are rather seldom.

: '''Marstrand's theorem:''' Let <math>\mu</math> be a Radon measure on <math>\mathbb{R}^{d}</math>. Suppose that the ''s''-density <math>\Theta^{s}(\mu,a)</math> exists and is positive and finite for ''a'' in a set of positive <math>\mu</math> measure. Then ''s'' is an integer.

== Preiss' theorem ==

In 1987 [[David Preiss]] proved a stronger version of Marstrand's theorem. One consequence is that sets with positive and finite density are [[rectifiable set]]s.

: '''Preiss' theorem:''' Let <math>\mu</math> be a Radon measure on <math>\mathbb{R}^{d}</math>. Suppose that ''m''<math>\geq 1</math> is an integer and the ''m''-density <math>\Theta^{m}(\mu,a)</math> exists and is positive and finite for <math>\mu</math> almost every ''a'' in the [[Support (measure theory)|support]] of <math>\mu</math>. Then <math>\mu</math> is ''m''-rectifiable, i.e. <math>\mu\ll H^{m}</math> (<math>\mu</math> is [[absolutely continuous]] with respect to [[Hausdorff measure]] <math>H^m</math>) and the support of <math>\mu</math> is an ''m''-rectifiable set.
